activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Studies show that nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood.
story:
Christopher sat on the spinning stool in front of the mirror and put on the fifth pair of frames, which made him look, in his own opinion, like a startled rodent. "These ones," he declared anyway, because the other four had been worse and his mother was already checking her phone for the third time.

"Those are perpendicular to your eyebrows," said Aviana, who worked the front counter on Saturdays and had opinions about everything, including his hair. "Tilted. Like a crooked picture frame."

"That's a style," Christopher said.

"That's a mistake," she said, and plucked them off his face and handed him a round tortoiseshell pair instead.

While his mother filled out the paperwork, Ms. Henry, the optometrist, came out of the back room with his chart. "Christopher," she said, "before you go, one question. Honest answer. On a normal Saturday, how much time do you spend outside?"

Christopher thought about this very carefully, because a normal Saturday involved a screen, a couch, and eleven straight hours of a game where he was currently ranked in the top two hundred players. "Some," he said. "A decent amount. Outdoors-adjacent."

Aviana snorted so hard she had to pretend to cough.

Ms. Henry just looked at him over her glasses. "Here's the thing. Studies show that nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood. So when I see a kid your age who needs glasses for distance, I can guess a lot about his weekends."

Christopher felt his face go warm. It was like she'd read his save file. He tested the idea, turning it over. "So if I go outside more now, does that fix it?"

"It's not a magic undo button," she said. "But it's a good habit anyway."

He slid the new frames on and looked at the wall of sunglasses across the store, which was suddenly crisp all the way to the corners instead of soft and foggy, and he had to admit the ceiling tiles had actual lines in them. "Travis is going to nominate me for biggest dork in the grade," he said, pulling out his phone to text him a selfie anyway.

The reply came back in eight seconds: a photo of Travis squinting at his own phone while holding a ruler, and the words "who's blurry NOW."

Aviana leaned over the counter. "Tell him what you learned," she said. "The weekend part. Word for word."

"He'll laugh."

"He squints at everything," she said. "Half the basketball team does. Go count."

Christopher thought of Travis, who never saw a scoreboard until they were three feet away, and of half his class rubbing their eyes after video marathons. He texted: "Up for the park tomorrow? I'll bring the ball. I can actually see the hoop now."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, slurping noodles such as ramen and soba is considered acceptable at the table rather than rude.
story:
Julia stood on the porch of Emmeline's grandmother's house holding a box of oranges wrapped in paper so shiny it squeaked. Through the door she could hear at least fifteen people talking at once, because tonight was Emmeline's grandmother's birthday, and Emmeline's whole enormous family had come from three different states.

"You take your shoes off first," Emmeline whispered, toeing off her sneakers into a row of sandals by the step. "Everybody does, even Uncle Rob, and he wears size thirteen."

Julia balanced on one foot, then the other, and set her shoes in the row. She had been rehearsing this moment since Tuesday, when her mother said, "You never show up to somebody's grandmother's birthday with your hands empty." Last weekend at her own family's gathering, her cousin had torn the wrapping paper off a gift in two seconds flat and lobbed it over his shoulder, but Emmeline had said that at her grandmother's house, gifts were opened quietly and the paper was folded. Two households, two sets of rules, and Julia meant to learn all of them before dinner.

She pressed the orange box into her hostess's hands with both arms and a small bow, the way Emmeline had demonstrated in the gym on Thursday. The grandmother's eyes crinkled, and she bowed back, lower than Julia expected, and said something that made the whole hallway laugh warmly.

Dinner was ramen, huge steaming bowls of it, and Julia had just lifted her chopsticks when the noise started. Slurrrp. Slurrrrp. It came from every side of the long table, from Emmeline's uncles, from the tiny cousins, even from Emmeline herself, loud and cheerful as a pack of happy engines. Julia froze with her noodles halfway to her mouth. At home that sound meant somebody was about to get the Look from Grandma. She glanced sideways to check whether anyone here was offended, and that was her first clue: nobody was. If slurping were rude, somebody would have frowned. Instead Emmeline's grandfather slurped again and sighed like a man receiving a medal.

So Julia formed a hypothesis, the way Mr. Sadeghi had taught them in science: if everyone did it, and nobody reacted, then the rule itself must be different here, not the people. She would test it once, quietly, and watch what happened. She drew in a modest slurp of broth.

"More," said Emmeline's grandmother, waving a ladle. "Louder! You eat like a shy little microbe!"

"A microbe can't slurp at all," Emmeline said. "I looked it up for Mr. Sadeghi's class. They're too small, and they don't have mouths, exactly."

"Then Julia must not eat like one," the grandmother declared, and the cousins chanted, "Not a microbe! Not a microbe!" Julia laughed so hard she nearly lost a noodle, then gathered up a truly heroic proportional quantity of noodles, about a third of the bowl, and slurped with everything she had. The table erupted in applause. Emmeline's grandfather raised his glass to her. Somewhere down the table an aunt called out that Julia was now officially family, and Emmeline kicked her gently under the table and whispered, "Told you."

After the cake, when the little ones were being herded toward the rooms where they would retire for the night, Emmeline's grandmother found Julia by the door, still holding her folded wrapping paper like a treasure. "Next year," she said, tapping the orange box, "you bring the noodles. I will teach you the big slurp."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: The 'fundamental attribution error', named by psychologist Lee Ross in 1977, is the habit of blaming someone's behavior on their character while overlooking the situation they were in.
story:
Savannah lay on her bed with the family group chat open on her phone, staring at the last message her cousin had sent, a photo of everyone at the lake. She recognized the towels, the cooler, her aunt's terrible hat. What she noticed most was the empty spot on the dock where Jordan usually sat, knees pulled up, grinning.

Jordan had skipped the sleepover on Saturday too. No explanation, just a text that said can't come, sorry, and then nothing for two days. Savannah had typed and deleted four replies. Her final answer had been a thumbs up, which felt cold even as she sent it.

"She just bails on everything now," Savannah said out loud to her phone. "She's become a flake."

Downstairs, her mom called that she was going to the store. A minute later the door shut, and the house went quiet except for the fridge humming. Savannah scrolled back through the chat, looking for proof of her theory. There was Jordan in June, participating in the cousin trivia game until midnight. There was Jordan in July, first to RSVP for the lake day. Then, three weeks ago, the messages just stopped.

That was a pattern, Savannah thought. But a pattern of what? Flakes didn't usually vanish overnight. Something had changed, and it wasn't Jordan's character. It was the situation, except she didn't know the situation.

She thought of Ms. Patel, who lived next door to Jordan and brought their family zucchini bread every August. Savannah pulled on her sandals and walked the two blocks, telling herself she was only returning a Tupperware container.

Ms. Patel answered the door with flour on her hands. "Savannah! Come in. Were you looking for Jordan? She's at the hospital with her grandmother, poor thing. The grandmother tore a tendon in her leg falling down the porch steps, and Jordan's been there every afternoon since, doing the dishes and reading to her."

Savannah felt her face go hot. "Every afternoon?"

"Every single one. She's keeping it quiet because her grandmother hates a fuss."

On the walk home, Savannah remembered a page she had photographed from her sister's psychology textbook because it looked interesting. She found it in her camera roll and read it again: the fundamental attribution error, named by psychologist Lee Ross in 1977, the habit of blaming someone's behavior on their character while overlooking the situation they were in. She had done exactly that. Twice.

Back in her room, she opened the chat with Jordan, who was not a flake, and who had a grandmother in a hospital bed. She typed slowly.

"I'm sorry I've been weird. Can I come with you tomorrow? I can bring cards."

The typing bubble appeared, then disappeared, then appeared again.

"Grandma cheats at gin rummy, just warning you."

Savannah grinned and grabbed a deck from the junk drawer.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Open-ended questions, which cannot be answered with just yes or no, usually get longer answers and keep a conversation going.
story:
Alice sat on her bed with her phone propped against a stack of library books, watching Noa's face fill the screen. "Okay, be him," Alice said. "I'll practice."

Noa straightened up and tried to look like someone who did not want to be there. "Hi, Alice."

"Hi. Do you like school?" Alice asked.

"Yes," Noa said, and then nothing. The silence stretched so long that Alice could hear the washing machine rumbling down the hall.

"That was it? That's the whole answer?"

"I answered your question," Noa said, grinning. "That's how Devon talks. Monroe calls him a human shrug."

Alice flopped backward onto her pillow and stared at the ceiling. The date was in two hours, at the coffee shop on Maple Street, and she had a whole list of questions like that one. Do you like movies. Do you have siblings. Every single one could be murdered with a single word. She sat up again. "Try this. Monroe, get in here."

Noa pulled Monroe into frame, and Alice ran a quick test. "Monroe, do you like pizza?"

"Obviously," Monroe said.

"Now this: what's the best pizza you've ever had?"

Monroe lit up like a struck match. "Okay, so there's this place my uncle took us to in the summer, and they do this charred crust thing, and I ate so much I nearly narrated my own downfall out loud on the drive home." He kept going for a full minute about sauce.

Alice wrote in her notebook: it's the question shape. Questions that can't be answered with just yes or no get longer answers and keep things going. She underlined it twice. It wasn't some mysterious mechanism she'd never crack; it was just a switch she could flip. She crossed out her whole list of yes-or-no questions and started over. What's a song you've had stuck in your head lately. What's the weirdest thing your grandmother has ever cooked you.

"Better," Noa said. "Although if he turns out to be volatile about pizza toppings, that's on you."

"It'll be fine," Alice said, but her stomach did a small flip anyway.

At the coffee shop, Devon showed up in a jacket that looked ironed by someone who cared about him, which made Alice feel a little steadier. They ordered, and when they sat down she asked, "What's the best thing you've ever built in shop class?"

Devon set down his cup. "Okay, you're going to think this is weird, but I made a lamp shaped like a lighthouse, and my mom put it in the hallway even though it's crooked." He talked through half his hot chocolate, waving his hands, and Alice nodded and asked what the hardest part had been.

When her cup was empty, Devon said, "This was better than I thought it would be."

"Same," Alice said, and slid her notebook, closed, across the table. "Next time you get to pick the questions."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Parallel lines like railway tracks or the two edges of a road look as if they meet in the distance, even though they never actually meet.
story:
Rosalie stared at her sketchbook, where her street looked like it had been flattened by a truck. The buildings leaned. The road ran straight off the page like a slide. "It's due Friday," Elie reminded her, tapping the assignment sheet. "One-point perspective, a street scene, the whole ninth grade hallway will see these."

"I know," Rosalie said. "That's the siege I'm under." Ms. Adebayo had pinned examples above the whiteboard, streets with lamp posts and shopfronts shrinking toward one single dot, but whenever Rosalie copied them, her lines wandered off like lost dogs.

She thought about the footbridge behind Avril's house, the one over the train tracks. Last autumn she and Avril had stood on it, arguing. "Look, the rails touch back there," Avril had insisted, pointing down the line. "They get closer and closer." Rosalie had squinted and refused. "Rails can't touch, or the train would crash. They're the same distance apart the whole way." Avril had stomped her foot on the bridge boards, and they'd gone inside still arguing, the question unresolved all winter.

Now, in the art room after school, Rosalie went still. The rails were the road. Two lines that never actually met could look as if they met in the distance. If she drew the edges of her road slanting toward one dot, the road would lie flat on the paper and still run away from the viewer, forever. She tested it on a scrap: a dot, two lines gliding toward it, a street that suddenly had depth. Her pencil would not stay still.

On Thursday she walked to Avril's, and they climbed to the footbridge to verify it. A freight train rattled beneath them, and they watched the rails hold their width under every wheel. "See?" Rosalie said. "They never meet. It only looks that way." She held up her finished drawing, street, shops, lamp posts, every edge obedient to her vanishing point. "That's the trick I used. Ms. Adebayo put a red star sticker on the corner."

Avril leaned over the rail with the drawing held beside the real tracks. "So the rails are like your road's edges," she said slowly. "Same thing."

"Exactly the same thing," Rosalie said. "Want me to show you how to put the dot in?"

Avril was already digging a pencil out of her backpack.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something.
story:
Hunter flopped onto the couch in the living room with his mom's phone and one goal: convince her to buy the Vortex X headset before Friday. It cost eighty-nine dollars, and every video he found said it was the best thing ever made. A famous streamer named BlazeVolt held it up to the camera and shouted, "This thing changed my life!" Two million people had watched that video. If two million people believed it, Hunter figured his mom should too.

He called Carson first. "BlazeVolt uses the Vortex X. Everybody's switching to it. It's revolutionary."

"Hang on," Carson said. "Revolutionary is just a fancy word they use to pump it up. Read the caption under the video."

Hunter scrolled down. At the end of a long string of hashtags, almost invisible, sat two letters and a symbol: #ad.

"That's it? Two characters?"

"Keep looking," Carson said, and hung up.

At school the next day, Hunter cornered Asees by the lockers. She was the most skeptical person in sixth grade, which was annoying, except when it was useful. "Did you know that in the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something?" she said. "BlazeVolt got that headset for free. He has to tell you, so he hides it in the hashtags."

Hunter wanted to dismiss her, but the #ad was still sitting there in his memory like a splinter. That afternoon he ran an experiment. He found five more glowing reviews of the Vortex X. Four of them had #ad buried somewhere. The fifth guy, some kid with forty subscribers, said the ear cushions fell apart in a month and the mic sounded like a dying robot. Hunter watched that video twice. Then he found five reviews of a cheaper headset, the Storm Pro. Two kids who seemed to actually own it said it was solid, and neither one had #ad anywhere.

He laid the two phones side by side on the living room carpet, videos paused, and texted his mom a list. Then he waited by the window, arms crossed, doing his best impression of someone who was not waiting.

His mom came home, dropped her bag, and looked at the list. "What's this?"

"Evidence," Hunter said. "The famous people got them free. The regular people say the cheap one lasts longer. I checked."

She raised an eyebrow. "Since when do you do research?"

"Since BlazeVolt tried to trick me with two letters and a hashtag."

His mom picked up the phone, tapped the Storm Pro video, and watched the kid with forty subscribers describe his broken ear cushions. Then she scrolled down, checking for something.

"No #ad," she said slowly.

"None. Zero." Hunter sat forward on the couch. "So... can we talk about Friday?"

His mom set the phone on the armrest and looked at him for a long moment.

"Order it yourself," she said, and slid her credit card across the coffee table.

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: In South Asia, crops sown at the start of the summer monsoon and harvested in autumn are called kharif crops, and rice is the main one.
story:
"So let me get this straight," Lillian said, spooning rice onto her plate at her grandmother's kitchen table. "In Punjab, you planted the rice and just... waited for rain?"

Her grandmother laughed and set down the teapot. "Not just rain. The first big rains of summer. Everything waited for them. The rice went into the ground when the monsoon began, and we harvested in autumn when it was tall and golden." She leaned forward. "There is a word for those crops. We called them kharif crops, and rice was the main one."

"Kharif," Lillian repeated, scribbling it on a napkin. She had a geography presentation on monsoons due Monday, and this was better than any website. Mr. Takahashi had told the class to find the hidden cause, the thing you couldn't see: air moving because of something invisible. She'd stared at diagrams all week and hadn't truly digest-ed the idea until now, sitting in her grandmother's kitchen, hearing about seedlings whose whole life depended on sky.

After dinner she spread a map of South Asia on the living room rug and frowned at it. The rain came every summer, her grandmother said, like clockwork. But why there? Why then? She needed to see the pattern for herself. Heaven and Colton were coming over tomorrow, and she refused to stand up there with an explanation she couldn't prove.

She went to the kitchen and filled a shallow baking pan with warm water, then set it at one end of the coffee table. At the other end she placed a dark cookie sheet she had left in the sun on the porch all afternoon. Then she cut a strip of tissue paper and dangled it above the cookie sheet. The paper fluttered toward the warm pan's side, no wait, she watched carefully, then flipped her notebook open. "The air over the hot dark sheet rises," she murmured, "and the air over the water slides in to take its place." That was the hidden cause. Over the ocean, that moisture-filled air replaced the rising hot land air, and when it piled up over the land, down came the rain.

The next morning, Heaven arrived first, with Colton behind her carrying a fan. "You said bring a fan," he said. "Explain."

Lillian already had the pans on the table, the tissue strip trembling in the still air. She aimed the fan at the water pan, cranked it on low, and the strip swung hard toward the cookie sheet, dancing. Heaven shrieked and pointed. Colton leaned in until his nose nearly touched it.

"Now watch," Lillian said, and turned the fan up one more notch.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: In Python, range(2, n) produces the numbers from 2 up to n minus 1, so it tries every possible divisor except 1 and n itself.
story:
Harper had promised Ms. Gagnon she would finish the prime-checking program over the weekend, and now it was Sunday afternoon at her grandfather's house, with the old laptop humming on the kitchen table and a pot of coffee breathing vapor into the cold air. She typed the program twice, ran it twice, and both times it told her that 7 was not prime, that 13 was not prime, that every number she tried was not prime. "That's not right," she said. "Seven is definitely prime."

Daven leaned over from the counter, where he was supposed to be drying dishes. "Maybe your loop is broken," he said. "Let me see." The screen showed her test: she looped through range(2, n + 1), and if any of those numbers divided n evenly, she printed "not prime." Harper stared at it. She could not see the loop working; it happened somewhere behind the screen, invisible, and she had to reason about it instead. She slowed down and traced one pass with n equal to 7. Try 2. Try 3. Try 4. Try 5. Try 6. Try 7, she thought, and stopped with a sudden feeling of dread. It tried 7. Of course it did. She was dividing 7 by 7 itself, and 7 goes into 7 evenly, every single time.

"Wait," she said slowly. "The range goes too far. It's testing n against itself." Daven frowned at the line. "So it's like checking whether a shoe fits by holding it against the exact same shoe," he said. "Equivalent sizes, always a match." Harper deleted the "plus one" and typed range(2, n) instead. Now the loop would run only up to n minus 1, which meant it tried every possible divisor except 1 and n itself. She held her breath and pressed enter. 7: prime. 13: prime. 9: not prime. She punched Daven's shoulder and ran it again on 2, on 51, on 101, laughing each time the right answer appeared.

Then she heard slow footsteps in the hall, and her grandfather shuffled in with his reading glasses pushed up on his forehead. "Finished your homework?" he asked. He had spent forty years as a machinist and did not trust computers, but he liked numbers, and he liked being right even more. "It works now," Harper said. "Try one." He planted a finger on the keyboard with great ceremony and typed 1.

The screen printed "prime." Her grandfather smiled and turned back toward the coffee pot, satisfied, while Harper sat frozen, staring at the answer she had never once tested and now dreaded to think about. "One is not prime," she said to Daven. "It's neither prime nor anything. Grandpa, come back."

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: The Grand Canyon is 277 miles (446 kilometers) long and over a mile deep at its deepest point.
story:
Blake stood at the edge of the old rock quarry, staring at the terraced walls below him, and wondered if this was what the Grand Canyon had looked like a few million years into its project. He had a science presentation tomorrow morning, and Mr. Warsame had been blunt about it: "If you can't explain how a river carves a canyon, Blake, you'll be explaining it to me again in summer school." That was a deadline Blake intended to beat.

"You're supposed to be researching, not just sweating," said Maddie, who had come along with a thermos of lemonade and zero sympathy. Melanie was already halfway down the gravel path, waving. "Come see this!" she shouted. "There's a stream down here, and it's doing something weird!"

The stream came out of the quarry wall in a thin brown ribbon and ran across the floor before vanishing into a pile of rubble. Where it ran, it had cut a channel into the gravel, and where it slowed near the pile, the water dropped its cargo of sand in a little fan-shaped heap. Blake crouched and watched. Fast water carried stuff away. Slow water put stuff down. That was it, wasn't it? The river was like a siege, patient and relentless, grinding at rock day after day, century after century, and whenever it slowed, it dropped its sediment and built something new. Over millions of years, that cycle could transform a flat plain into a canyon. He needed to test it.

He borrowed Maddie's lemonade, took a swig to make room, and poured a steady stream across a slab of soft, crumbly shale beside the channel. For a moment nothing happened. Then a dark line appeared where the water ran, and grains of shale flaked loose and rode the current downstream. "Look at that," Blake breathed. "It's carving. Right now. On camera, if I'd brought my phone."

"Congratulations, you've invented the Grand Canyon in miniature," Melanie said. "Except the real one is 277 miles long. That's 446 kilometers, according to the book I'm holding, which is heavy, so hurry up." Blake tried to picture 277 miles. He'd once biked six miles and thought he might die. Then he tried to picture the deepest part, over a mile straight down, and his stomach did a slow, delighted roll, like leaning over a balcony. A hole in the ground that a river made. A river that looked exactly like this unimpressive brown trickle, just given a few million years and no quit in it at all.

"So the water is the predator?" Maddie asked, watching the stream gnaw at its bank. "Like, predatory water?" Blake considered it. "Sort of, but slow. The slowest predator ever. It just never stops, and the rock does." He scooped up a handful of the sand from the little fan downstream, where the water had set it down, and let it pour through his fingers. Carry, drop, carry, drop. Millions of years of that. He grinned, wiped his hands on his jeans, and started climbing back up the path to plan his poster.

"Tomorrow," he told the trickle, pointing at it like a villain, "you're going to make me sound smart." The stream, unbothered, kept gnawing at the shale.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Airplane mode turns off a phone's radio signals, including the cellular connection it uses for calls and texts.
story:
The phone store smelled like new plastic and cold air, and Ariana held the box like it might burst. Her mother had finally agreed, on one condition: the account was in her name, and she would have to authorize every app Ariana downloaded. "That means nothing goes on this phone without me knowing," her mother said at the counter, tapping the screen where Ms. Khoury, who lived three doors down and worked weekends here, held out a stylus. "Sign there."

Ms. Khoury walked them through the basics, then handed the phone over. "Set a passcode nobody can guess. Not your birthday." Ariana chose a random number, four digits she'd never used before, and the screen unlocked with a soft click. Crossing the parking lot, she waited for the walk signal at the concrete median between the lanes of cars, phone warm in her pocket, and by the time they reached home she had already texted Inara and Keiran to tell them the news.

Then came the strange part. Keiran replied within minutes: FINALLY. But nothing came from Inara. Ariana checked her signal bars, full. She restarted the phone, counted the bars again, and sent another message. An hour passed, then two. She began to suspect the worst, that Inara was upset with her, that she'd somehow been left out of something. That evening a message finally arrived, but not from Inara. It was from Keiran, and it said: "Inara says she's been texting you all afternoon from her grandma's house. She thinks you're ignoring her. She's really mad."

Ariana stared at it. If Inara's messages weren't arriving, and her own signal was fine, then the problem had to be on the other end. She remembered something Ms. Khoury had said while setting up the phone, almost in passing, that Ariana had half noticed at the time: "Airplane mode turns off the phone's radio signals, including the cellular connection it uses for calls and texts." She thought about Inara's grandma, the flight to see her last month, Inara's habit of fiddling with settings. On a hunch, Ariana called Inara's number. Straight to a strange tone, no ringing, as if the phone were switched off entirely, even though Keiran swore Inara's battery was full.

Ariana texted Keiran one instruction: "Tell Inara to swipe down and look for the little airplane icon at the top of her screen. Tell her to tap it so it turns gray." She waited by the window, watching the streetlight flicker on, phone face-up on her desk like a small black mirror.

Forty seconds later the screen lit up with a flood of messages, eleven of them, timestamped across the whole afternoon, the last one reading "FINE I'm sorry, it WAS on, it's off now, I feel so dumb." Ariana laughed out loud, typed "it's okay, airplane mode got you," and hit send. Then she glanced at her own signal bars to make sure her reply had gone through, and saw, sitting quiet in the corner of her screen, a small white airplane.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Running directly behind another runner shelters you from the wind, so following someone on the first lap can save energy for the finish.
story:
The eight-hundred metres was two laps, and Emile had blown both of them last time. He had sprinted the first lap like it was the only lap, and by the second curve his legs had turned to wet sand while Ryker sailed past him at the finish. Mr. Chan had watched from the fence and said only one thing afterward: "The race starts at the four hundred." Emile turned that over all week. The problem was invisible. He could not see energy leaking out of him, but something was taking it, and he meant to find out what.

At practice he tried an experiment. Lap one, he told himself, would be boring on purpose. He would hold back even when every instinct screamed at him to chase the leaders, because instinct had already cost him one race. He asked Chanelle to stand at the two-hundred mark with a stopwatch and call out his split, so he would know if "slow" was actually slow or just felt slow.

Race day came gray and gusty. The rules prohibited headphones, spiking, cutting inside, all the usual things, but nothing about the wind, which shoved at everyone equally. Emile stayed calm through the first curve, and then, on the back straight, it hit him full in the face, a wall of moving air that made each stride heavier than the last. Ryker was three metres ahead, shoulders rolling, driving straight into it. And Emile noticed something odd. Behind Ryker, the air went strangely still, as if the wind stopped at his back and started again at Emile's chest. He slid in close, tucked himself into that quiet pocket, and kept Ryker's jersey as a target.

The pocket held for the whole back straight. Emile's breathing stayed level while runners around him sagged and dropped back one by one. At the bell lap he was still there, fourth wheel in a line of three, and Chanelle's voice cut through the noise: "Sixty-eight! You're on pace!" He had never gone through four hundred that slowly, and he had never felt this good doing it.

The twist came at the final curve. Ryker glanced over his shoulder, and Emile understood, with a jolt that was almost corrosive to his plan, that Ryker had known he was there the entire time and had been towing him along, confident he could drop him anytime. Ryker surged. Emile surged with him, and this time, this time, there was something left in his legs. The second lap, the one that had always been stolen from him, belonged to him instead. He came off the last bend level with Ryker, then ahead, then clearly ahead, and crossed the line with his arms up and his lungs burning pleasantly.

Afterward, bent over with his hands on his knees, Emile felt Ryker clap his back. "You figured out the wind, didn't you," Ryker said, not quite a question. "Took me three races to find that pocket." Emile grinned, still gasping, and pointed at the empty back straight, where the flags snapped and the grass bent flat. "Best seat in the house," he said.

activity: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
knowledge_domain: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
fact: When two triangles share a side, that side is equal to itself, a step proofs call the reflexive property.
story:
Romy sat at the kitchen table with her geometry notebook open and a pencil that had already lost its eraser. The retest was Monday morning, and Ms. Tang had written one comment at the top of her quiz in red pen: "You have all the pieces. Look at the picture again."

"It's like she's speaking in code," Romy muttered, drawing the figure for the fifth time. Triangle ABC and triangle ADC sat back to back, and she was supposed to prove them congruent using side-angle-side, which needed two pairs of sides and the angle between them.

Hadley leaned over from the counter, where she was attempting to make toast without setting off the smoke alarm. "You've been staring at that page so long your juice has evaporated. Want me to look?"

"You got a sixty-two on that quiz."

"A sixty-two is a diplomatic sixty-two," Hadley said, puffing up like a tiny diplomat. "I'm immune to your insults."

"First, that's not what diplomatic means, and second, come here anyway." Romy tapped the drawing. "I've got side AB equals side AD. I've got angle BAC equals angle DAC. Side-angle-side needs one more pair of sides, and I only see one left that I can't prove."

Hadley squinted. "Which one?"

"BC and DC. There's nothing telling me they're equal. It's like the proof wants a sock I don't own."

Hadley stole the pencil and drew a circle around the middle of the figure. "What's this line, then? AC?"

"That's the diagonal. It doesn't count, it's just... there." Romy stopped. The toast popped up, ignored. "Wait. Wait wait wait."

"Say words."

"AC belongs to both triangles." Romy grabbed the pencil back so fast she nearly stabbed the toast. "It's the same segment. So side AC equals side AC because it's literally the same line."

"That sounds like cheating."

"It's not cheating, it's..." Romy flipped through her notes until she found Ms. Tang's list of reasons. "Reflexive property. When two triangles share a side, that side is equal to itself, a step proofs call the reflexive property. It's on the list of legal moves and I skipped it every single time."

She wrote the proof out in four lines, fast, then read it aloud like a court verdict. "AB equals AD, angle BAC equals angle DAC, AC equals AC by the reflexive property. Therefore the triangles are congruent by side-angle-side."

Hadley picked up her toast, saluted with it, and said, "So the side you needed was hiding inside the triangles the whole time."

"Sharing a border with both of them." Romy drew a tiny crown on point C. "King of the reflexive property."

Then she turned the page and froze. "Hadley. The next problem is the same figure flipped upside down."

Hadley bit her toast. "Then flip your crown."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Carbon has atomic number 6, so every carbon atom has six protons in its nucleus.
story:
Paige spread the battered periodic table across the workbench, weighting one corner with a hammer and the other with a coffee can of screws. The garage smelled like motor oil and cut grass, and Anais was already pacing between the shelf and the door, drumming a pencil against her palm.

"I need this done before Saturday," Anais said. "Ms. Nair said the quiz retake is Monday morning, and if I fail again, my mom makes me quit robotics club. Do you get how much that would humiliate me? I'm the one who built the claw."

"You're going to pass," Paige said. "We're going to crack this thing tonight. Sit down."

Anais sat on an overturned milk crate and held up the pencil. "Start with something real. This. It says graphite on the label. So what's graphite even made of?"

Paige ran her finger down the printed table, past the colorful blocks, hunting the letters C. There. Carbon. And in the corner of its box, a small number. "Six," she said slowly. "The atomic number is six."

"Meaning what, though? I can't see a number inside a pencil."

Paige stared at the box. That was the whole problem, wasn't it. Atoms were too small to see, so the table had to be a kind of map, a code. The number had to tell you something. She flipped the sheet over and found the fine print at the bottom, the little legend she'd almost thrown away. She traced it with her finger and then sat back so fast she nearly knocked over the coffee can.

"Anais. Atomic number six means every carbon atom has six protons in its nucleus. That's the rule. That's what the number is for."

"Protons," Anais repeated, leaning over the bench. "So the graphite in this pencil, all of it, every speck, is carbon with six protons?"

"Every single atom." Paige grabbed the pencil and tapped it against the table like a gavel. "It's like the table is handing you a count. Pick any element, read the number, and you know its protons."

"Okay, hypothetical question," Anais said, eyes narrowing. "The robot claw. The gripper pads are plastic, and you keep calling plastic a polymer. Could I count protons in a polymer too, if I knew what elements were in it?"

"Try me," Paige said.

Anais snatched the sheet and dragged it toward the crate, hunting down oxygen, hydrogen, whatever she could find, muttering numbers. Paige flipped the pencil over and wrote 6 on the back of her hand. From the driveway came the sound of a basketball bouncing, then stopping.

"Hey!" Anais called through the garage door, holding the sheet up like a trophy. "Mom's going to let me keep the club. Tell her carbon has six protons, I'll say. Watch me ace this thing."

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: When patching a tube with glue-on patches, the glue must be left to dry until it is no longer wet before the patch is pressed on.
story:
Lucas crouched on the back porch with his bike upside down, wheels in the air like a beetle, and slid the first tyre lever under the rim. The lever popped the bead loose with a snap he felt in his fingers. Somewhere in the shed a wasp droned like a tiny turbine, and he paused until it wandered off toward the fence.

The front tyre had gone flat halfway to Alia's house yesterday, and he had walked the bike home with the wheel hissing a little on every rotation. Now he pulled the tube out and lowered it into a bowl of soapy water, squeezing sections slowly. Why did punctures hide like this? Bubbles would tell him. A cluster of them rose near the valve, gleaming, and he marked the spot with the ballpoint pen from his dad's workbench.

He found the patch kit where Mr. Mendoza had left it after fixing his own bike last summer. Lucas remembered standing at the fence watching him: the smell of rubber cement, the little orange tube, Mr. Mendoza pressing a patch on and saying, "The tricky part is the waiting." Lucas, eleven then, had not asked what that meant.

He roughed the marked spot with the sandpaper, brushed away the dust, and spread a thin layer of glue over it, thin and shiny like jam on toast. Then he sat there holding the patch, staring at the wet glue, and wondered what the waiting was actually for. What changed between wet and not wet? He had no way to see inside it. He could only test it. So he peeled the foil off a patch, pressed it onto the shiny glue right away, rubbed it hard with his thumb, and pumped the tube up fat. It held air. He grinned, worked the tube back inside the tyre, levered the bead over the rim, and pumped until the tyre was firm.

He rode to Alia's street, and somewhere past the corner he felt the soft squish return, a wobble in the handlebars like the bike was shrugging. By the time he reached her driveway the tyre was flat again, and when he peeled the patch loose it came away with almost no effort, glue still tacky underneath. Alia leaned her own bike against the wall and watched him turn the patch over in his fingers. "It just let go?" she asked. "Basically the moment I sat on it," Lucas said. He rolled the wheel, thinking. The patch had seemed fine in his hands. But on the road, less than a mile, it had peeled off. The difference couldn't be the patch or the glue, because both were the same as in the kit. The only thing he'd controlled badly was time.

Back home he sanded a fresh spot, spread the glue, and this time set the tube on the porch rail and watched it change. The shine dulled, the wet look faded, and when he touched the very edge with one fingertip it felt dry. Only then did he press the patch on and rub it flat with the lever handle. He pumped the tyre until the pump grew stiff, spun the wheel, and listened to the even tick of the valve going round. Then he wheeled the bike down the steps and said to Alia, who had followed him back, "Get your shoes. we're testing this properly."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing guitar strings repeatedly makes the fingertips sore at first; with regular practice, the skin toughens into calluses and playing hurts less.
story:
Charles pressed his index finger down on the E string for the tenth time and winced. The tip had gone from red to a shiny pink, and every chord in Ms. Toussaint's garage made it feel like the string was biting him.

"I'm retiring this guitar," he announced, setting it on the workbench between a coffee can of screws and a jar of pencils. "A week of this is enough."

Braydon, who had come over to listen, picked up the guitar and turned it over. "Retiring it? You found it in your grandpa's garage like four days ago. You haven't even learned a whole song."

"Because it hurts." Charles held up his hand and pointed at his fingertips, one by one, like evidence at a trial. "Here, here, here, and especially here. Grandpa played this thing for fifty years. How did he stand it?"

Braydon ran his thumb along the strings. "Maybe his fingers were different."

Charles looked at the photograph taped inside the garage door, the one of his grandpa on a porch with this same guitar. In the picture, his grandpa's left hand was blurred because it was moving, and the fingers looked thick, almost swollen. Charles pulled the photo off the door and held it under the window light. "Look at his fingertips. They're not swollen. That's skin. Tough skin." He thought about the workers who built houses near the school, how their hands changed because of what they did every day. Maybe the pain wasn't a warning to stop. Maybe it was a stage.

"Fine," Charles said, taking the guitar back. "Then it's not retiring. It's practicing." He played the chord progression again, badly, and the pain flared, but he kept going. By the time Adelynn arrived on her bike, he had run through it thirty times, and the tips of his fingers had gone numb enough that he barely noticed.

"Your conscience is clear now?" Adelynn asked, laughing. "You were going to quit your grandpa's guitar."

"I wasn't quitting. I was resting." He flexed his fingers. "It still hurts, though. It's supposed to hurt for a while, I think. Then the skin gets tough and it stops." He looked down at his hands, which looked exactly like a fourteen-year-old's hands, nothing like the ones in the photograph. Not yet. Maybe not for months.

He strummed the chord one more time, and even though it buzzed against the fret, he held the shape until the sound rang all the way to the rolled-up garage door.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: Galileo studied motion by rolling balls down gentle ramps, which slowed the motion enough for him to time it.
story:
The skate park had one thing Jonathan's kitchen did not: a long, gentle concrete slope where the ramps curved down to the flat. He stood at the top of it holding a tennis ball, while Safa crouched near the bottom with her phone stopwatch ready and Isa chalked a line on the ground every metre.

The problem was Monday. Mr. Schneider wanted a distance-time graph, drawn from real measurements, showing the speed of a rolling ball in metres per second. Jonathan had missed the class trip to the science museum, where everyone else had used the exhibit with the long wooden ramp. He'd chosen a skate competition instead, and now he had no data and two days.

"Start it at the top," Safa called. "Don't push it."

He let the ball go and it trickled down the slope, slow enough that Safa could click the stopwatch each time it crossed a chalk line. They wrote the times in Isa's notebook: one metre in just under a second, two metres in a bit less than two, three metres before three seconds were up. So the ball was covering more ground each second. It was speeding up, and the numbers proved it even though nobody could see speed itself.

"Isa," Jonathan said, squinting at the notebook, "what did that plaque at the museum say again?"

Isa pulled out her phone and found the photo she'd taken. "Galileo studied motion by rolling balls down gentle ramps, which slowed the motion enough for him to time it." She shrugged. "That's the whole sign."

Jonathan read it twice. The museum ramp was gentle on purpose, because a steep drop would be too fast to time with the tools they had. He looked at the slope under his feet, gentle in exactly the same way, and felt like he'd stolen a piece of the museum without going. "So this isn't a cheap substitute," he said. "It's the actual method. Galileo would have loved this place."

"Galileo couldn't drop in," Isa said, which was true, and which made Jonathan feel a strange empathy for a man dead for centuries, a man who had all the ramps and none of the kick turns.

They ran the ball six more times so the graph would have solid points. Safa plotted the numbers while Jonathan and Isa finally did the skating they'd given up most of the afternoon for. On his last run before dark, Jonathan bailed hard on the flat and sat there holding his ankle, laughing anyway, while Safa waved the finished graph above her head like a flag. "Your points make a curve," she shouted across the park. "It's beautiful. Also, your ball was faster at the bottom."

"It was always faster at the bottom," Jonathan called back. "Now I can prove it."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: The earliest eyeglasses were made in central Italy around 1290.
story:
Hannah had memorized the playground so she could pretend she didn't need glasses: four steps from the gate to the hopscotch grid, then a straight line to the swings, where the blur of the slide waited on her right. She was counting steps when Ariel crashed into her from behind.

"You're getting them today, right?" Ariel said. "After school? The optical shop next to the bakery?"

"After school," Hannah admitted. She had spent a week trying to conceal how bad her eyes had gotten, tipping her head to read the whiteboard, copying Ariel's homework numbers when the board dissolved into fog. But the eye doctor had ended all that, and now a pair of purple frames with her name on the order slip sat waiting.

Blakely swung off the monkey bars and landed beside them. "My cousin got glasses last year and said everything looked like the world had been drawn with a fat marker. Edges everywhere. Too many edges."

"That's the good part," Ariel argued. "Edges are information."

Hannah sat on the swing but didn't pump. What bothered her wasn't the edges. It was a thought she'd been chewing on since the doctor's office, where a poster on the ceiling had shown a painting of old monks with little circles balanced on their noses. The words beneath had been too blurry to read, but one line had printed itself into her memory before it smeared: the earliest eyeglasses were made in central Italy around 1290. Which meant before that, nobody had them. She was thirteen and could barely find her own locker combination without squinting, and somehow entire centuries of people had read, built cathedrals, kept records, all without glasses. It didn't seem coherent. There had to be a hidden reason, a pattern she was missing.

At lunch she ran a test. "Blakely. If you couldn't see well and there were no glasses anywhere, what would you do?"

"Quit reading," Blakely said immediately.

"Exactly. But people didn't quit. They copied manuscripts for hundreds of years before 1290." Hannah laid out her reasoning like a chain: some jobs, like scribes, probably went to people whose eyes happened to be good, the way tall kids end up blocking the basketball net. "So nobody needed glasses, because the nearsighted people were doing something else. Sweating in a field doesn't take sharp eyes."

Blakely frowned. "What about old scribes? Their eyes got bad eventually."

"Maybe they got promoted to the guy who dictates," Hannah said, "and a young guy with good eyes held the pen."

Ariel pointed a fry at her. "You realize you just spent lunch solving a problem from seven hundred years ago."

"Somebody has to," Hannah said.

After school, her mother drove her to the shop. While the optician made tiny adjustments to the purple frames, Hannah finally asked the question she'd been saving, and the optician nodded and tapped a book open on the counter, showing the same painting of the monks. "That's right," the optician said. "Central Italy, around 1290."

Hannah put the glasses on. The world snapped into focus so hard she grabbed the counter: individual leaves on the tree outside, the exit sign, a sign she had never once been able to read, a price list with every letter sharp and separate. She walked out onto the sidewalk and turned toward the bakery, where a boy about her age was squinting at a menu taped to the window, holding it two inches from his nose.

"Can't read it?" Hannah asked.

"Not without going blind," the boy said.

She looked at him, then at the menu, then at him again. "What year do you think it is?"

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means a faster speed.
story:
Elliot dragged the old workbench lamp to the middle of the garage and plugged it in. Yusuf unrolled the paper across the concrete, and Sasha set two tennis balls on the floor by the door.

"We raced three times," Yusuf said. "I won twice."

"One of those doesn't count," Sasha said. "You jumped the start."

"Neither of us can prove anything. That's the problem." Elliot crouched and marked a start line with chalk, then a line every metre up to eight metres. "Ms. Mercado lent us the stopwatch and the graph paper. We time the ball, we plot the distance against the time, and the graph tells us who's faster. No arguing."

Sasha rolled her ball first. Elliot clicked the stopwatch and called out each metre mark as the ball crossed it. Yusuf wrote down the numbers, his pencil digging into the paper. They rolled each ball three more times, moving the lamp when their shadows blocked the chalk marks. Sasha kept asking to prolong the test, wanting a fifth roll, a sixth, and Elliot kept shaking his head.

"Four is enough. More rolls just make us tired and sloppy."

Then he plotted it. Sasha's points climbed the graph in a nearly straight line. Yusuf's did the same, but his line leaned steeper against the grid. Elliot ran his finger up each one and stopped at the top.

"Wait." He tapped Yusuf's line. "Look which one is steeper."

"So?" Yusuf leaned over the paper.

"Steeper means faster. That's how you read this thing. Your line gets higher in less time." Elliot tapped Sasha's line next, flatter, and her face went tight.

"That's not right," she said. "I beat you in the second race."

"You jumped the start, remember? That's a head start, not speed." He set the two balls side by side on the chalk line. "Look at it again. Same race, same lines, one graph."

Sasha took the pencil and traced both lines with it, twice, slowly. Her instinct was still to argue, Elliot could see it, but the lines sat there on the grid, plain as the chalk marks on the floor. Steeper and flatter. Two lines, one winner.

"Fine," she said. "Best out of five rolls tomorrow. Fresh graph."

"Deal." Yusuf grinned. "Speed runs in my family, you know. Hereditary."

Sasha snatched her ball off the floor. "Prove it on paper."

Elliot folded the graph along the crease and slid it into his back pocket. Outside, the streetlight hummed on, and he clicked off the garage lamp.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Muscles in a limb kept still in a cast weaken and shrink, which is why an arm often looks thinner when the cast comes off.
story:
Evan discovered the problem on a Tuesday, three weeks into wearing the cast, when Camden signed his name and added the words "get well soon, soldier." Evan laughed, then stopped. "Actually, when this comes off, I go back to being a civilian," he said, tapping the plaster with his knuckle. "A civilian with one weird arm." He laid both arms flat on the lunch table, and even through the cast he could tell the left one was doing nothing all day while the right one opened his locker, wrote his homework, and held his sandwich. Nothing about the cast had been explicit about that. The doctor had said "keep it still," and Evan had obeyed like it was a law, but now he wondered what "still" was doing underneath.

That night he tried an experiment. He couldn't see inside the cast, so he had to test from the outside. He pressed the fingers of his left hand together as hard as he could, ten squeezes, then ten more, then a rest. His forearm ached in a deep, tired way, which had to mean something in there was still working. He wrote it in his notebook: "Squeezes, 20. Arm tired." The next morning he told Abby at the bus stop. "I think muscles that don't move shrink," he said. "My grandpa's leg was skinny after his boot came off, remember? He said the muscles weaken and shrink when a limb stays still in a cast." Abby squinted at the cast as if it might confess. "So you're exercising a leg you can't see." "Basically," Evan said. She offered to count his squeezes at lunch, which mostly meant yelling numbers while he gripped a stress ball she'd stolen from her brother.

He kept the notebook going. Forty squeezes. Sixty. He tried flexing at the elbow a tiny amount, felt the twinge, and backed off, because Ms. Adeyemi, his neighbor, had spotted him doing it from her porch and said, "Careful. The bone sets the schedule, not you." She was watering her tomatoes and didn't lecture further, so Evan adjusted: fingers only, slow and steady, every single day. Camden started bringing his own stress ball so Evan wouldn't feel ridiculous squeezing alone in the cafeteria. On a bad Thursday when Evan's arm ached and he skipped a whole day, Abby didn't scold him. She just wrote "one off day, fine" in the notebook and drew a small, unimpressed potato next to it, which Evan understood to imply that tomorrow counted double. He did doubles.

The morning the cast came off, the nurse used the little buzzing saw and Evan held his breath. Then his arm was out in the fluorescent light, and his stomach dropped. It was thinner than the other one. Noticeably, ridiculously thinner, pale and soft-looking next to his right forearm. "See?" he said to his mom, holding both arms side by side. "I told you. Muscles kept still in a cast weaken and shrink. That's why it looks like this." The nurse nodded. "It's normal," she said, "everybody's arm looks like that after a cast. It comes back with use."

Back home, Evan lined up on the living room floor for the first real test: push-up position, hands flat, weight forward. His left arm shook like a kitten's. He did four push-ups and collapsed onto the carpet, laughing. Camden, sprawled on the couch, called out, "Five's your civilian record. Beat it." Evan set his hands, pressed up once, twice, felt the thin arm wobble and hold.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: Robert's Rules of Order, a guide to running meetings fairly, was first published in 1876 by U.S. Army officer Henry Martyn Robert.
story:
Blake had called three meetings of the Playground Improvement Club, and all three had ended the same way: Amy and Eileen shouting about swings while the treasurer's report went unread and everyone's little brothers wandered off to the tire swing. Something was wrong, and it wasn't the members. Blake noticed the pattern. Whenever two people started talking at once, nobody had a rule for whose turn it was, so the loudest voice won, every time.

The problem was invisible, which bothered him. He couldn't see "no rules," the way he could see a broken swing chain. But he could test the idea. If turns were the issue, then something that forced turns should fix it.

At home he found a dusty green book on the shelf above the garage fridge, left over from his grandfather's boxes. The spine said Robert's Rules of Order. Blake flipped it open and read the first page, which announced that the book was a guide to running meetings fairly, first published in 1876 by U.S. Army officer Henry Martyn Robert. An army officer, Blake thought, which explained why the book treated speaking out of turn like a military offense.

Saturday morning he carried the book to the playground, where Amy and Eileen were already arguing about whether the endangered milkweed patch by the fence counted as club business. "Before we fight," Blake said, "we're trying something." He held up the book. "Robert's Rules of Order. It's a guide to running meetings fairly, and it was first published in 1876 by a U.S. Army officer named Henry Martyn Robert."

"Okay, grandpa," Amy said.

"It has an agenda," Blake said. "Items in order. You restrict yourself to the item on the list. Old business first, then new."

Eileen squinted at the milkweed. "So I can't just yell about the fence?"

"You can move that it goes on the agenda. Then we vote."

The first ten minutes were rough. Eileen tried to discuss the fence during the treasurer's report, and Amy talked over her, and Blake raised his hand at his own meeting, which felt ridiculous but worked. The book said one speaker at a time, recognized by the chair, and once Blake actually enforced it, the shouting dropped off like a engine quitting. The club discovered it had four dollars and a jar of bottle caps, and agreed, calmly, that the milkweed was club business by a vote of three to one. The one was Amy, who abstained on principle, though nobody knew which principle.

Blake's test had worked. The hidden cause was turns, not people. He wrote the next meeting's agenda in pencil on the back of his hand: welcome, minutes, treasurer, milkweed, swings, adjourn.

At the end Amy leaned over the book. "Henry Martyn Robert," she read. "Army officer. Wrote a whole book about meetings."

"Published it in 1876," Blake said. "People have been talking over each other for a long time."

Eileen raised her hand. "Motion to move the swings to item one."

"Seconded," said Amy, already raising her hand too.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Health agencies recommend scrubbing hands with soap for at least 20 seconds, including after changing a diaper and before preparing food.
story:
Gabriel stood in Ms. Tran's backyard with a two-year-old named Milo and a list of instructions stuck to the fridge, and so far the instructions were winning. The list said lunch at noon, nap at one, and no juice after two, but Milo had other plans, which mostly involved a wading pool, a hose, and a diaper situation that Gabriel did not want to think about ever again. He carried Milo inside, changed him on the towel Ms. Tran had left out, and stared at his own hands like they belonged to a stranger.

On the bathroom mirror there was a sticker, the kind the health clinic handed out at school. Gabriel had walked past it a hundred times without reading it, but now the words seemed aimed straight at him: scrub hands with soap for at least 20 seconds, including after changing a diaper and before preparing food. Twenty seconds. He had no idea how long that was. When he washed his hands normally, it took about four seconds and involved a lot of splashing. He tried counting one-Mississippi, but he lost track somewhere around nine because Milo was trying to flush the toilet.

Then he remembered his little sister's song about the ducks that fly south every winter, the migratory ones, and how his sister sang it roughly nine hundred times a day. He hummed it once, scrubbing the backs of his hands and between his fingers like the sticker showed, and it felt close to twenty seconds but maybe short. He hummed it twice. That felt right. Milo banged on the toilet lid along with the second round, which Gabriel decided to accept as moral support.

In the kitchen, Milo refused to sit still, so Gabriel set him up with crayons at the table while he cut grapes in half, because the list said halve the grapes, underlined twice. Milo drew a long squiggly line and pointed at it proudly. "That's the intestine," Gabriel said, squinting, because he'd flipped through Milo's picture book about the body earlier and the winding pink tube was the one page Milo would sit still for. Milo nodded like a professor. The drawing also seemed to depict a duck, or possibly Gabriel, which was less flattering.

They were halfway through lunch, Milo with grape-smeared cheeks and Gabriel with a growing sense that maybe he could actually do this, when Ms. Tran came home early. She looked at the clean kitchen, the sleeping-wet-but-happy toddler, and Gabriel washing his hands a second time after wiping Milo's face. "Were you humming in here?" she asked. "Twice," Gabriel said, holding up soapy hands. "The whole duck song." She laughed and pulled out her wallet.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: The marking 'a tempo' tells players to return to the original speed after the music has slowed down or sped up.
story:
Jayden's fingers hovered over the keys of the old upright piano in the basement of Temple Beth Shalom, where the youth band rehearsed on Thursdays. Mr. Campbell-Brown had finally trusted him with the piano part for the community concert, and tonight was the last practice before Sunday.

"Again from measure twelve," said Kyleigh, who conducted the group and wanted, more than anything, to win a solo spot at the spring recital. "Jayden, you're dragging."

Jayden played the passage again. He slowed down at the rit., just like the sheet music said, and the melody felt heavy and mournful, which he thought sounded beautiful. But Kyleigh stopped him with a flat palm.

"You stay slow the whole rest of the piece," she said. "The band comes back to speed and you just keep crawling behind us."

Dominick, tuning his violin nearby, leaned over the piano and tapped the page. "What does that mean?" He pointed at two small words above measure twenty.

Jayden looked at the marking. A tempo. He'd been reading music for three years, but he'd never paid attention to that phrase. He thought back to last week, when the whole band had sounded scrambled and he'd blamed the drums. Maybe the trouble had been him the entire time. His intuition said there was a pattern here: the piece slowed down, and something had to bring it back.

He adjusted the bench, took a breath, and tried the passage as an experiment. He slowed at the rit., letting the music stretch like elastic, and then, at the words a tempo, he snapped back to the original speed. Kyleigh's eyes widened. The band locked together, Dominick's violin soaring over the top, and for eight measures everything fit.

"That's it," Kyleigh said. "A tempo. Go back to the original speed after you slow down." She scribbled a note on her own music, then glanced toward the sanctuary doors where the music director was listening. Jayden noticed her straighten up, playing her violin line with extra shine, and he wondered whether she was hoping for that solo more than she'd ever admit.

On Sunday, waiting in the wings of the sanctuary while the candles were lit, Jayden traced the marking with his finger one more time. He remembered choosing to ignore the small words two weeks ago, when skipping details had felt easier, and he hadn't even known he was doing it. He couldn't decide yet whether that old habit was gone or only hiding. Kyleigh nudged his elbow.

"Measure twelve," she whispered. "Ready?"

Jayden set his hands on the keys.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A result that shows the hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result and is worth reporting.
story:
Ethan stood in aisle nine of Dalby's Hardware, holding two different kinds of foam insulation and pretending he could tell them apart by weight. "The conventional one," he announced, "is the boring one."

"That's not what conventional means," said Elyane, who was there because her mother had sent her for a plunger and she had decided Ethan's crisis was more interesting. "It just means the usual kind."

"The usual kind failed. Twice." Ethan dropped both sheets back on the shelf. "My project is doomed. Maybe I should just conquer something else. Like a different aisle."

The project was a solar oven, and his hypothesis had been that the mirror-lined box would get hotter than the foil-lined one. He had measured the mirror box at sixty-one degrees and the foil box at sixty-seven. His prediction had lost, and the science fair was Thursday.

Evelyne appeared at the end of the aisle holding a plunger like a scepter. "Mom sent me to find Elyane. Instead I found a tragedy."

"It's not a tragedy," Ethan said, and then, quieter, "It kind of is. I predicted mirrors would win. Foil won. What am I supposed to do, present a project that says I was wrong?"

He flashed back to Tuesday, when he'd stood in Mr. Costa's classroom holding the thermometer like it had personally betrayed him. "Seventy-two in the mirror box today, Mr. Costa. Even worse." He had waited for his teacher to look disappointed. Instead Mr. Costa had leaned against the lab bench, flipping through Ethan's data table, and said, "You know what my favorite kind of result is? A wrong one. A result that shows the hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result, and it's worth reporting." Then he had handed the table back and wandered off to argue with someone about their volcano.

Ethan had thought he was being polite. Now, staring at foam sheets, he turned it over in his head. A wrong result was still a real result. His data wasn't broken. It was data. Six trials, careful measurements, one clear pattern, and the pattern pointed the opposite way from his guess. That wasn't nothing. That was the whole point of measuring instead of just guessing.

"Actually," he said slowly, "I'm going to present the foil thing. Wrong hypothesis, real result."

"That's the saddest victory speech I've ever heard," Evelyne said.

"It's not a victory speech. I still need a presentation board." Ethan snapped his fingers at Elyane. "Does this store sell poster board, or is that too conventional?"

"It's aisle four," called Mr. Costa, who had been restocking duct tape two bays over the entire time and had heard everything. "And I want front row Thursday. Bring the foil."

Ethan grabbed a cart. "Foil box, coming through."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Muscles grow stronger during recovery after training, not during the workout itself, so rest days are part of getting better.
story:
The gymnasium smelled like rubber mats and humid air, and Parker had the rebound record board in front of him again, counting names. Eddie's name had climbed for three weeks straight, then stopped, then dropped. That was the part Parker couldn't stop turning over. Eddie hadn't missed a single practice. He came early for shooting drills and stayed late for sprints, every day, and somehow his times were getting slower. Parker chewed the end of his pen and wondered what could make hard work go backward. A rule that you couldn't see was doing something, and he wanted to know what it was.

He started keeping a small chart in the back of his science notebook. Eddie's sprint times, day by day, plus a mark for every day Eddie trained. Then Parker added his own times, because he needed a comparison, and his own chart was almost boring: steady, tiny improvements, week after week. The interesting difference wasn't effort. Eddie trained every single day, and Parker took Sundays off, mostly because his mom made him help clean the garage. He stared at the two columns. Was it possible the missing day was the helpful part? It felt like asking whether the hole in a doughnut was what made it taste good.

"You're watching me like I'm a lab experiment," Eddie said after practice, towelling off his hair.

"Sort of," Parker admitted. "You're getting slower and I think I know why. Muscles get stronger during recovery, not during the workout itself. Rest days are part of getting better. You never take one."

Eddie snorted. "Rest is for people who violate the schedule. I'm not skipping."

"Then just try it once," Parker said. "One Sunday. Lie around. Then time yourself Monday." He held out the stopwatch like it was a bet.

On Monday morning the gym was quiet except for the squeak of their shoes. Parker ran first and posted his usual time. Then Eddie crouched at the baseline, jaw set, and pushed off. Parker clicked the watch and watched the numbers fall, and when Eddie crossed the line, his time was two tenths faster than his best from the week before. Eddie stood with his hands on his knees, breathing hard, staring at Parker like the floor had opened up.

"Two tenths," Eddie said. "From doing nothing?"

"One Sunday of nothing," Parker said, and grinned, and wrote it on the chart.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed that Snowball, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, could move in time to music and adjust when the tempo changed.
story:
Olivier stood in front of the mirror at the clothing store holding up a shirt the colour of a traffic cone. "No," he said, and put it back.

He was shopping for the fall dance, his first one, and the rack of acceptable shirts was starting to dwindle. There were the traffic cone, three plaid ones, and a grey shirt that made him look like a middle-aged accountant. His mother, parked on a bench by the fitting rooms with her phone, had already vetoed the plaid. Olivier was beginning to suspect she was right.

"Olivier?" Abygaelle from science class appeared beside him, holding a stack of sweaters. "You going to the dance?"

"Maybe," he said, which was a lie. He was going. The whole grade had voted on the theme by ballot, and "Midnight in Paris" had beaten "Neon Rave" by four votes, and his mother had already bought nonrefundable shoes.

"I can't dance," Abygaelle said. She held up her phone. "Watch this. It's a sulphur-crested cockatoo called Snowball. He moves in time to music. And when they change the tempo, he adjusts. Scientists showed that in 2009, a team led by Aniruddh Patel."

On the small screen, a white bird with a yellow crest bobbed and swung its head, hitting the beat better than anyone at Olivier's school ever had. "He's better than Johan," Olivier said.

"Johan dances like a broken sprinkler," Abygaelle agreed. "The thing is, if a bird can keep the beat, I figure I can too."

Olivier looked at the bird, then at the store's ceiling speakers, which were playing something with a steady thump to it. Here was a testable idea. If the cockatoo could track a beat, a thirteen-year-old with a functioning nervous system should manage at least a nod. He shifted his weight. One, two, three, four. His shoulders got involved. It felt ridiculous, in a store, next to a girl from science class, but the beat was right there, regular as a pulse, and he found it.

Abygaelle watched him with her chin in her hand. "Not bad. You're stiff, but you're on time."

The cashier leaned over her counter. "You two want the fitting room, or are you auditioning?"

Olivier stopped. Abygaelle did not. She kept bobbing, obstinate, right through the cashier's stare, until the woman gave up and returned to folding the traffic-cone shirts.

"See you at Midnight in Paris," Olivier said. He took the grey accountant shirt into the fitting room, shut the door, and, facing the mirror, started counting again.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Naive realism is the belief that we see the world as it really is, so people who disagree with us must be uninformed or biased.
story:
Elijah raised his hand before Mr. Nowak had even finished putting the photo on the board. It showed the school garden with its sunflower bed flattened, and one bee still drifting from blossom to blossom, pollinating whatever was left standing. "Zachariah's dog did it," Elijah said. "He told me his dog got out Tuesday night."

"Actually," Zachariah said, "I said the dog got out. I never said it flattened anything. That could have been random weather, wind, anything." He was leaning forward like this mattered to him, because it did. His mother ran the garden club, and she had already blamed his dog in a group chat.

Mr. Nowak held up a hand. "Before we decide, let's hear what people see in the photo." Cleo said the stems were broken low, which meant something pushed through, not wind. Someone else said the paths were too narrow for a big dog. Elijah kept arguing for the dog, and he noticed something odd: the more evidence piled against him, the more certain he felt. He caught Cleo's eye, and she gave him a look that said, notice what you're doing.

After class, he found her by the water fountain. "Okay, here's my theory," he said. "I think everybody believes they see the world as it really is. And if somebody disagrees, you figure they must be uninformed or biased. Zachariah's mom thinks the dog did it, my story matches hers, so everyone on the other side looks dumb to me." Cleo nodded slowly. "There's a name for that," she said. "It's called naive realism. I read it on my brother's psychology poster." Elijah turned that over. He had been so sure. But was Zachariah's mother really biased, or was she just interpreting the same night differently, the same way Elijah's own memory of Tuesday was honestly kind of blurry?

He decided to test it. At lunch he asked Zachariah, "What time did the dog get out, exactly?" Zachariah checked his phone. "Nine fifteen. And here's the thing." He swiped to a security clip from their back gate. The dog, at nine fifteen, trotted out, trotted back, and lay down. The flattening must have happened later. But then, at the edge of the frame, a shape moved through the moonlit sunflowers, low and slow. "Is that," Elijah said, leaning closer, "a goat?" Zachariah grinned. "Mr. Nowak's goat. It got loose Tuesday. He asked us not to tell anyone until he fixed the fence."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Two players can have the same average while one is steady and the other swings between great and terrible games, since an average hides how spread out the results are.
story:
The group chat lit up at 7:03 p.m., right after Coach posted the roster rules: four players per team for the Saturday tournament, and the last spot on Gavin's team was still open. Lyndon sent a screenshot of two players' stats, both from the rec league across town. "Same average," he typed. "Both 18 points a game. So it doesn't matter, right?"

Gavin frowned at his phone. His mom was telling him to stop staring at the screen while the bees she kept in the garden went about pollinating her tomato flowers, but he barely heard her. Something about those two stat lines bothered him, and he couldn't say what. He scrolled through the league site himself, game by game, and found it. "Wait," he typed. "Look at the actual games."

Liyana was first to reply. "What games?" Gavin sent a photo of the score sheet he'd copied into his notebook. Player One: 18, 19, 17, 18, 18. Player Two: 36, 4, 30, 2, 18. "Same average," he wrote. "But look. One of them is steady every single night. The other swings between great and terrible." Lyndon sent a row of thinking emojis, then: "Okay, that's weird." Liyana sent: "So the average hides that?"

"Basically," Gavin typed, then deleted it, because he wanted to show them instead of just claiming it. He started a poll in the chat: "Who do you pick?" He added, "Think about what happens if the tournament is one bad day, not five games." Lyndon voted steady player.
